H1.text: Two hall tickets. One says seat three comma five, the other says five comma three. Same two numbers. Same seat?

H2.text: No. They are two different desks. Swap the numbers, and you sit in someone else's seat.

H3.text: Aarav learned this on his first exam day.

H4.text: So when does the order of two numbers matter?

H5.text: The answer is the ordered pair, the building block of this whole chapter.

O1.text: Last time, every element of A cross B was a pair in round brackets. Let us look closely at that pair.

O2.text: An ordered pair is two objects in a fixed order, inside round brackets, with a comma between them.

O3.text: The one on the left is the first element. The one on the right is the second element.

O4.text: For a seat in the hall, the first number is the column. The second number is the row.

L1.text: Watch the seat finder. For three comma five, walk three columns across, then five rows up.

L2.text: For five comma three, walk five columns across, then three rows up. A different desk.

L3.text: Now keep the second number at three, and let the first number, a, count up.

L4.text: The blue dot is a comma three. Its twin, three comma a, is the swapped pair.

L5.text: They land on the same desk only once, when a is three. Swapping changes the seat, unless both numbers are equal.

S1.text: Side by side. Curly brackets make a set, and order does not matter. The set three, five equals the set five, three.

S2.text: Round brackets make an ordered pair, and order is everything. Three comma five is not five comma three.

K1.text: Now you try. Is two comma two a proper ordered pair, even though both entries are the same? Pause and think.

K2.text: Yes! It is the desk in column two, row two. A pair may repeat an entry.

E1.text: So when are two ordered pairs equal?

E2.text: In NCERT words: two ordered pairs are equal if and only if the corresponding first elements are equal, and the second elements are also equal.

E3.text: In symbols: a comma b equals c comma d, exactly when a equals c, and b equals d.

E4.text: Both checks must pass. Three comma five and three comma four share the first element, but they are different pairs.

T1.text: Remember this. In an ordered pair, position is meaning. Swap the entries, and you get a new pair.

D1.text: Now a big result. Is A cross B the same set as B cross A?

D2.text: Step one. Take A as one and two, and take B as just three.

D3.text: Step two. A cross B is one comma three, and two comma three. The first elements come from A.

D4.text: Step three. B cross A is three comma one, and three comma two. Now the first elements come from B.

D5.text: Step four. One comma three is not three comma one. So the two sets differ, though each has two elements.

D6.text: So A cross B and B cross A differ, unless A equals B, or one set is empty.

R1.text: Pairs can grow. Three objects in a fixed order make an ordered triplet.

R2.text: A cross A cross A holds every triplet with entries from A. If A has two elements, that is two times two times two, eight triplets.

R3.text: And R cross R, pairs of real numbers, is every point on a graph sheet. Each point is one ordered pair, x comma y.

W2.text: If two x minus one comma y plus three equals five comma one, find x and y.

W3.text: Step one. Equal pairs have equal first elements. Two x minus one equals five.

W4.text: Step two. Add one, then halve. x equals three.

W5.text: Step three. The second elements are equal too. y plus three equals one.

W6.text: Step four. Take away three. y equals minus two.

W7.text: Check. Two times three, minus one, is five. Minus two plus three is one. Both match.

X2.text: If x squared comma y plus one equals nine comma four, many students write x equals three, and stop.

X3.text: But minus three squared is also nine. So x is three or minus three, and y is three. Two answers: three comma three, and minus three comma three.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In PUC exams: equal ordered pairs, find x and y. In JEE Main, inside questions that count ordered pairs.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A is the set of integers whose square is at most four. How many ordered pairs a comma b in A cross A are different from b comma a? Pause and solve.

A2.text: A is minus two, minus one, zero, one and two. That is five integers.

A3.text: So A cross A has five times five, which is twenty five ordered pairs.

A4.text: A pair equals its swap only when a equals b. That is five pairs.

A5.text: Twenty five minus five leaves twenty pairs that change when swapped.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. If x plus two comma four equals five comma two y, find x and y.

Y3.text: Two. Is the set one, two equal to the set two, one? Is one comma two equal to two comma one?

Y4.text: Three. If A is p and q, and B is r, are A cross B and B cross A equal?
